screens.title: Load Balancing Strategies and Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build an intuitive, practical understanding of load balancing. A load balancer is the traffic cop that distributes client requests across a server pool so no single server becomes a bottleneck. You will learn why a load balancer is essential once you add more servers, how policies and algorithms guide request routing, and how features like health checks and session persistence affect reliability and user experience. We'll compare simple approaches like Round Robin to dynamic strategies such as Least Connections and IP Hash, and you'll see where session stickiness is useful and where it causes trouble. A concrete example you'll revisit is configuring Nginx to perform Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, and simple health checks for three backend servers named web1, web2, and web3. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to justify an algorithm choice for an interview: explain the trade-offs, describe how unhealthy servers are removed, and propose a migration from sticky sessions to stateless services using an external session store. Keep this lens in mind: pick the policy that matches your traffic pattern and service requirements.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives give you a clear roadmap for mastering load balancing in distributed systems. First, you'll be able to explain the fundamental role of a load balancer: how it coordinates traffic across horizontally scaled servers and why it is essential to avoid single-server bottlenecks. Second, you will identify and describe common load balancing algorithms like Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash, explaining when each suits particular traffic patterns. Third, you will understand health checks and session persistence; why active probes keep traffic away from failing servers, and how sticky sessions maintain in-memory state at the cost of flexibility. Finally, you will design a basic load balancing setup for a web application, weighing algorithm choices, session handling, and health check strategies against traffic variability. Each objective ties a practical skill to a reasoned trade-off so you can justify decisions during interviews or in design reviews.

screens.title: What is a Load Balancer?
screens.narratorSegment: A load balancer is the network component that routes client requests across multiple servers to maximize throughput, reduce latency, and ensure availability. Think of it as a traffic cop stationed in front of a fleet of identical servers: it decides which server should handle each incoming request based on an algorithm and the current health of each server. The important goals are straightforward: prevent any one server from becoming a bottleneck, maintain responsiveness for users, and continue serving traffic when servers fail. A concrete example is a web storefront scaled to three servers; the load balancer ensures that incoming shopping requests are distributed so that no single machine gets overwhelmed during a sale. A common misconception is to assume the load balancer always improves latency — in practice it can add a small proxy overhead, so you must balance routing benefits against this cost. Key takeaway: the load balancer doesn't create capacity by itself, but it makes horizontal capacity usable and reliable. How will you explain this role in an interview? Emphasize throughput, latency, and the ability to mask failures from clients.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A load balancer routes requests across servers to balance load, improve responsiveness, and increase availability.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
What is a Load Balancer?
A short conceptual definition and why it matters.
Traffic-cop analogy

The load balancer selects which server gets each request so the overall system stays fast and available. It is responsible for distribution policy and observing server health.

Why this matters
  • Enables horizontal scaling to be effective.
  • Masks server failures from clients.
  • Allows you to apply routing policies for different traffic types.
Key Takeaway

A load balancer coordinates traffic; it enables reliable, scalable use of multiple servers but does not replace capacity planning.

Concrete example
Imagine three identical web servers behind a load balancer. During peak traffic, requests are distributed so nodes share work. If one node fails health checks, the balancer stops sending it traffic and the remaining nodes carry the load.
Client
Load Balancer
Server pool (web1, web2, web3)
Common misconception: a load balancer magically increases capacity. It only utilizes existing capacity more effectively and improves resilience by removing unhealthy nodes.

screens.title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancers can operate at different layers of the OSI model, and the most common distinction is between Layer 4 and Layer 7. Layer 4 load balancers make forwarding decisions based on transport information such as TCP or UDP ports and IP addresses. They forward connections without looking inside the application payload, which makes them fast and low-overhead. By contrast, Layer 7 load balancers inspect application-level data like HTTP headers, URLs, and cookies, enabling routing rules that depend on content, hostnames, or session cookies. A practical example: if you need URL-based routing to send /api requests to a different pool than /web, you need Layer 7. A misconception is to treat Layer 4 as obsolete — it remains the best fit when you need minimal latency and simple connection forwarding. Key takeaway: pick Layer 4 for raw speed and simple forwarding, and Layer 7 when you need application-aware routing and richer policies such as cookie affinity or header inspection. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing means layer 4 for fast transport-level forwarding; layer 7 for application-aware routing using headers, urls, and cookies.. In practical terms, transport-level forwarding versus application-aware routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Layer 4 vs Layer 7
Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
Choose the layer based on routing needs and latency requirements.
Layer 4 (Transport)
Forwards TCP/UDP connections without inspecting application data. Low overhead and high performance.
  • Use when minimal latency matters.
  • Cannot route based on HTTP headers or URL paths.
  • Examples: simple TCP forwarding, network load balancers.
Common misconception: Layer 4 is always simpler; in some cases you lose needed routing control.
Layer 7 (Application)
Inspects HTTP headers, URLs, or cookies and makes intelligent routing decisions based on application data.
  • Use when you need URL routing, host-based rules, or cookie affinity.
  • Higher flexibility at the cost of additional processing overhead.
  • Examples: application load balancers, HTTP proxies.
Key trade-off: flexibility versus processing overhead.
When to use L4
When to use L7
Example: route /api to specific pool

screens.title: Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin
screens.narratorSegment: Round Robin distributes requests sequentially to each backend server in turn. For example, with servers A, B, and C, requests go A, B, C, A, B, and so on. The advantage is its simplicity and predictable distribution over time. The drawback is it ignores server load and capacity; a slow or busy server still receives an equal share of requests. Weighted Round Robin extends this idea by assigning integer weights to each server that reflect processing capacity. If server A has weight 3 and servers B and C have weight 1, A receives three times as many requests as B or C. This is helpful in heterogeneous fleets where some machines are more powerful. A common misconception is to assume weights guarantee perfect capacity matching — weights are coarse and do not account for transient load or long-lived connections. In interviews, explain when Weighted Round Robin improves fairness and when dynamic algorithms like Least Connections may be preferable for variable request durations. Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin means round robin is easy and fair over time; weighted round robin adjusts distribution by server capacity but does not adapt to changing runtime load.. In practical terms, simple distribution strategies and capacity-aware weighting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow Round Robin & Weighted
Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin
Sequential distribution and capacity-aware weighting explained with examples.
Round Robin
Requests cycle through servers in order. Good for homogeneous servers and steady short requests.
Example: three servers A, B, C — request order: A, B, C, A, B, C. Works well if request processing time is similar.
Misconception: equal distribution means equal load. Not true if request durations vary widely.
Weighted Round Robin
Assign weights to indicate capacity. Servers with higher weights receive proportionally more requests.
Example: weights A=3, B=1, C=1 results in A getting three times the traffic of B or C. Helpful when servers differ in CPU or memory.
Limitation: weights are static and do not reflect transient conditions like sudden CPU spikes or long-lived connections.
Pro tip

Use Weighted Round Robin when you know capacity differences in advance, but consider dynamic algorithms if load fluctuates unpredictably.

screens.title: Least Connections and Least Response Time
screens.narratorSegment: Least Connections sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections. This makes it more adaptive than Round Robin for scenarios where connections have variable durations, such as WebSockets or long-polling. The algorithm helps prevent a busy server from receiving more traffic while others sit idle. A related approach is Least Response Time, which routes to the server with the lowest observed latency or fastest recent response time. This requires actively measuring response times and making routing decisions based on performance. A practical example: in a data A P I where some requests query slow reports and others are fast, Least Connections will prefer servers currently handling fewer long queries. A common misconception is that these algorithms remove the need for capacity planning — they help distribution but cannot eliminate overloaded clusters. Key takeaway: dynamic algorithms improve responsiveness under heterogeneous workloads but add measurement complexity and possible oscillation if not tuned. Least Connections and Least Response Time means least connections adapts to active connection counts; least response time uses measured latency to select healthier backends.. In practical terms, dynamic algorithms that respond to server state and latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Least Connections adapts to active connection counts; Least Response Time uses measured latency to select healthier backends.

content.html:
Process Flow Dynamic Algorithms
Least Connections and Least Response Time
How dynamic algorithms balance variable-duration work and latency-sensitive requests.
Least Connections
Selects the server with the fewest active sessions. Especially useful when connection durations vary widely.
Example: long-polling clients hold connections; Least Connections routes new clients to less-busy servers so those servers don't become overloaded.
Misconception: it perfectly balances CPU or memory. It balances connections, not other resource usage.
Least Response Time
Routes requests to servers with the lowest measured latency to improve perceived performance.
Example: if server B responds faster than A and C, new requests go to B until response time changes. Requires active monitoring of response metrics.
Trade-off: measurement overhead and potential route oscillation if measurements are noisy.
Check your understanding
Which algorithm would you choose for a service with many long-lived connections? Why?

screens.title: IP Hash and Session Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: IP Hash uses a hash of the client's IP address to consistently route a client to the same backend server as long as the server pool is unchanged. This creates session persistence without additional state in the load balancer. Session persistence, also called sticky sessions, ensures that a user's entire session is handled by the same server — important if session state is stored in memory on the application server. For example, a shopping cart kept in R A M on Server A will remain accessible if subsequent requests from the same client are always routed to A. However, sticky sessions carry significant trade-offs: they can cause uneven distribution if certain client IPs generate disproportionate traffic, and they make maintenance and failover more complex — if the sticky server fails, its sessions are lost. A best practice for large scale is to externalize session state to a distributed cache so any server can handle any request. When discussing this in an interview, contrast immediate practicality with future refactor plans toward stateless services. IP Hash and Session Persistence means ip hash provides stickiness by mapping client ips to servers, but can cause uneven load and complicate failover; prefer external session stores when possible.. In practical terms, sticky sessions, their uses, and their trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: IP Hash provides stickiness by mapping client IPs to servers, but can cause uneven load and complicate failover; prefer external session stores when possible.

content.html:
Definition IP Hash & Sticky Sessions
IP Hash and Session Persistence
Why stickiness exists and when to avoid it.
How IP Hash works
Compute a hash from the client's IP and use it to select a backend. The same IP maps to the same server if the pool is stable.
Example: client IP 10.1.1.5 hashes to Server B, so subsequent requests go to B until the server pool changes.
Trade-offs
  • Pros: simple stickiness without server-side state sharing.
  • Cons: uneven distribution if a few IPs are heavy traffic sources.
  • Cons: if a server fails, sticky sessions are lost unless state is externalized.
Best practice: prefer stateless servers with a shared session store for scalable systems.
Common Mistake

Relying on sticky sessions for long-term scale. Plan to externalize session state when possible to simplify scaling and failover.

screens.title: Health Checks: Detecting and Removing Unhealthy Servers
screens.narratorSegment: Health checks are periodic probes the load balancer sends to backend servers to determine whether they are healthy. Typical checks include TCP connection tests or HTTP GETs to a /health endpoint that verifies not only the server process but also critical dependencies, such as database connectivity. When a server fails to respond, exceeds a timeout, or returns error status codes, the balancer marks it unhealthy and stops sending new traffic to it. Once the server recovers and passes subsequent checks, it rejoins the rotation. A concrete example: configure Nginx upstream servers with max_fails and fail_timeout so that after three failed attempts within 30 seconds a server is temporarily removed. A common mistake is to check only that the web process is up; instead the health endpoint should run lightweight checks against external dependencies. Key takeaway: robust health checks reduce user disruption by ensuring traffic only goes to servers that can fully serve requests. Health Checks: Detecting and Removing Unhealthy Servers means active probes verify server and dependency health; failing servers are removed until they recover, improving reliability for new requests.. In practical terms, how probes work and common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Health checks
keyIdea.text: Active probes verify server and dependency health; failing servers are removed until they recover, improving reliability for new requests.

content.html:
Process Flow Health Checks
Health Checks: Detecting and Removing Unhealthy Servers
Design probes that verify process and critical dependencies to avoid false positives or negatives.
How probes work
  • Send TCP or HTTP probes at intervals.
  • Mark a server unhealthy when failures exceed a threshold.
  • Return the server to rotation after successful checks.
Example configuration pattern: set max_fails and fail_timeout so a server that fails three probes in 30 seconds is marked down. This prevents transient glitches from immediately removing nodes while still protecting clients from persistent failures.
Checklist for a good health endpoint
  1. Verify the server process is responsive.
  2. Confirm connections to critical dependencies like databases.
  3. Keep the check lightweight to avoid overloading the server.
Key Takeaway

Health checks should validate both the application and its dependencies to avoid routing traffic to servers that cannot fully serve requests.

screens.title: Designing a Basic Load Balancing Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a basic load balancing setup requires matching the algorithm and features to traffic patterns and application requirements. Start by categorizing traffic: is it stateless short requests, long-lived connections, or sessionful interactions? For stateless APIs, dynamic algorithms like Least Connections are usually a good fit because any server can handle any request. For long-lived connections, Least Connections avoids packing too many persistent sessions on one node. If your application holds session state in memory, you may need session persistence and IP Hash or cookie-based affinity, recognizing this will complicate scaling and failover. When servers have different capacities, use Weighted Round Robin to account for heterogeneity. Always include health checks that validate dependencies, and plan how state will be preserved during maintenance or failure (for example, migrate sessions to a shared cache). The concrete Nginx example in this chapter shows upstream blocks for Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin and a basic max_fails pattern for passive health detection. In interview answers, walk through these choices and explain the trade-offs. Designing a Basic Load Balancing Setup means match algorithm to traffic type, add health checks, account for server capacity, and prefer stateless services with external session stores when possible.. Code Walkthrough Nginx Config
Hands-on: Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
A practical starter configuration for Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin and simple failure handling.
Starter configuration
# Part 1: Basic Round Robin upstream backend_servers_round_robin { server web1:8000; server web2:8000; server web3:8000; } server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://backend_servers_round_robin; } } # Part 2: Weighted Round Robin upstream backend_servers_weighted { server web1:8000 weight=2; server web2:8000; server web3:8000; } server { listen 81; location / { proxy_pass http://backend_servers_weighted; } } # Part 3: Health Check (passive) upstream backend_servers_health_check { server web1:8000 weight=2 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s; server web2:8000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s; server web3:8000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s; } server { listen 82; location / { proxy_pass http://backend_servers_health_check; } }

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build an intuitive, practical understanding of load balancing. A load balancer is the traffic cop that distributes client requests across a server pool so no single server becomes a bottleneck. You will learn why a load balancer is essential once you add more servers, how policies and algorithms guide request routing, and how features like health checks and session persistence affect reliability and user experience. We'll compare simple approaches like Round Robin to dynamic strategies such as Least Connections and IP Hash, and you'll see where session stickiness is useful and where it causes trouble. A concrete example you'll revisit is configuring Nginx to perform Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, and simple health checks for three backend servers named web1, web2, and web3. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to justify an algorithm choice for an interview: explain the trade-offs, describe how unhealthy servers are removed, and propose a migration from sticky sessions to stateless services using an external session store. Keep this lens in mind: pick the policy that matches your traffic pattern and service requirements.

These objectives give you a clear roadmap for mastering load balancing in distributed systems. First, you'll be able to explain the fundamental role of a load balancer: how it coordinates traffic across horizontally scaled servers and why it is essential to avoid single-server bottlenecks. Second, you will identify and describe common load balancing algorithms like Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash, explaining when each suits particular traffic patterns. Third, you will understand health checks and session persistence; why active probes keep traffic away from failing servers, and how sticky sessions maintain in-memory state at the cost of flexibility. Finally, you will design a basic load balancing setup for a web application, weighing algorithm choices, session handling, and health check strategies against traffic variability. Each objective ties a practical skill to a reasoned trade-off so you can justify decisions during interviews or in design reviews.

These objectives expand into practical assessment skills you will use in interviews. You'll prepare to explain algorithm trade-offs with concrete examples: why Round Robin is simple but blind to load, why Weighted Round Robin helps heterogeneous fleets, and why Least Connections adapts to connection duration. You'll be able to describe health-check design: what a probe should validate, how to set failure thresholds, and how removing unhealthy servers affects in-flight sessions. For session persistence, you'll explain sticky sessions, the roles of IP Hash or cookie-based affinity, and the modern alternative: move session state out of the application into a distributed cache so any server can serve requests. Finally you'll practice designing a small Nginx reverse-proxy configuration for three servers. These skills let you defend choices, show trade-offs, and propose migration paths in system-design conversations.

A load balancer is the network component that routes client requests across multiple servers to maximize throughput, reduce latency, and ensure availability. Think of it as a traffic cop stationed in front of a fleet of identical servers: it decides which server should handle each incoming request based on an algorithm and the current health of each server. The important goals are straightforward: prevent any one server from becoming a bottleneck, maintain responsiveness for users, and continue serving traffic when servers fail. A concrete example is a web storefront scaled to three servers; the load balancer ensures that incoming shopping requests are distributed so that no single machine gets overwhelmed during a sale. A common misconception is to assume the load balancer always improves latency — in practice it can add a small proxy overhead, so you must balance routing benefits against this cost. Key takeaway: the load balancer doesn't create capacity by itself, but it makes horizontal capacity usable and reliable. How will you explain this role in an interview? Emphasize throughput, latency, and the ability to mask failures from clients.

Load balancers can operate at different layers of the OSI model, and the most common distinction is between Layer 4 and Layer 7. Layer 4 load balancers make forwarding decisions based on transport information such as TCP or UDP ports and IP addresses. They forward connections without looking inside the application payload, which makes them fast and low-overhead. By contrast, Layer 7 load balancers inspect application-level data like HTTP headers, URLs, and cookies, enabling routing rules that depend on content, hostnames, or session cookies. A practical example: if you need URL-based routing to send /api requests to a different pool than /web, you need Layer 7. A misconception is to treat Layer 4 as obsolete — it remains the best fit when you need minimal latency and simple connection forwarding. Key takeaway: pick Layer 4 for raw speed and simple forwarding, and Layer 7 when you need application-aware routing and richer policies such as cookie affinity or header inspection. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing means layer 4 for fast transport-level forwarding; layer 7 for application-aware routing using headers, urls, and cookies.. In practical terms, transport-level forwarding versus application-aware routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Round Robin distributes requests sequentially to each backend server in turn. For example, with servers A, B, and C, requests go A, B, C, A, B, and so on. The advantage is its simplicity and predictable distribution over time. The drawback is it ignores server load and capacity; a slow or busy server still receives an equal share of requests. Weighted Round Robin extends this idea by assigning integer weights to each server that reflect processing capacity. If server A has weight 3 and servers B and C have weight 1, A receives three times as many requests as B or C. This is helpful in heterogeneous fleets where some machines are more powerful. A common misconception is to assume weights guarantee perfect capacity matching — weights are coarse and do not account for transient load or long-lived connections. In interviews, explain when Weighted Round Robin improves fairness and when dynamic algorithms like Least Connections may be preferable for variable request durations. Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin means round robin is easy and fair over time; weighted round robin adjusts distribution by server capacity but does not adapt to changing runtime load.. In practical terms, simple distribution strategies and capacity-aware weighting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Least Connections sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections. This makes it more adaptive than Round Robin for scenarios where connections have variable durations, such as WebSockets or long-polling. The algorithm helps prevent a busy server from receiving more traffic while others sit idle. A related approach is Least Response Time, which routes to the server with the lowest observed latency or fastest recent response time. This requires actively measuring response times and making routing decisions based on performance. A practical example: in a data A P I where some requests query slow reports and others are fast, Least Connections will prefer servers currently handling fewer long queries. A common misconception is that these algorithms remove the need for capacity planning — they help distribution but cannot eliminate overloaded clusters. Key takeaway: dynamic algorithms improve responsiveness under heterogeneous workloads but add measurement complexity and possible oscillation if not tuned. Least Connections and Least Response Time means least connections adapts to active connection counts; least response time uses measured latency to select healthier backends.. In practical terms, dynamic algorithms that respond to server state and latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IP Hash uses a hash of the client's IP address to consistently route a client to the same backend server as long as the server pool is unchanged. This creates session persistence without additional state in the load balancer. Session persistence, also called sticky sessions, ensures that a user's entire session is handled by the same server — important if session state is stored in memory on the application server. For example, a shopping cart kept in R A M on Server A will remain accessible if subsequent requests from the same client are always routed to A. However, sticky sessions carry significant trade-offs: they can cause uneven distribution if certain client IPs generate disproportionate traffic, and they make maintenance and failover more complex — if the sticky server fails, its sessions are lost. A best practice for large scale is to externalize session state to a distributed cache so any server can handle any request. When discussing this in an interview, contrast immediate practicality with future refactor plans toward stateless services. IP Hash and Session Persistence means ip hash provides stickiness by mapping client ips to servers, but can cause uneven load and complicate failover; prefer external session stores when possible.. In practical terms, sticky sessions, their uses, and their trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Health checks are periodic probes the load balancer sends to backend servers to determine whether they are healthy. Typical checks include TCP connection tests or HTTP GETs to a /health endpoint that verifies not only the server process but also critical dependencies, such as database connectivity. When a server fails to respond, exceeds a timeout, or returns error status codes, the balancer marks it unhealthy and stops sending new traffic to it. Once the server recovers and passes subsequent checks, it rejoins the rotation. A concrete example: configure Nginx upstream servers with max_fails and fail_timeout so that after three failed attempts within 30 seconds a server is temporarily removed. A common mistake is to check only that the web process is up; instead the health endpoint should run lightweight checks against external dependencies. Key takeaway: robust health checks reduce user disruption by ensuring traffic only goes to servers that can fully serve requests. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's summarize the essentials you should retain. First: a load balancer coordinates traffic to use multiple servers effectively; it improves throughput and masks failure but does not substitute for capacity planning. Second: Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin are simple and useful when traffic is predictable and servers are homogeneous or weights are known; they do not react to transient server load. Third: dynamic algorithms like Least Connections or Least Response Time adapt to runtime conditions and are better for variable-duration requests, but they require careful measurement and tuning. Keep these three core ideas ready to explain during interviews with a short example and a trade-off for each.
